Research question: Does having children decrease engagement in extramarital affairs? I analyzed the Fair affairs dataset (601 married individuals) using both descriptive statistics and a logistic regression model predicting any extramarital affair during the past year. Average affair score (0–12 scale) was 1.69 for respondents without children and 1.36 for respondents with children. The proportion reporting at least one affair was 0.257 without children and 0.247 with children. In the logistic regression controlling for gender, age, years married, religiousness, education, occupation, self-rated marriage quality, and income, the coefficient for having children was -0.022 (p = 0.916) on the log-odds scale. A negative coefficient indicates that, holding other factors constant, having children is associated with a lower probability of reporting any affair. Both mean affair scores and proportions suggest that respondents with children have slightly lower engagement in affairs than those without children. Given the sample size, observational design, and possible unmeasured confounders, I treat these results as associative rather than strictly causal.

I analyzed the Fair affairs dataset (601 married individuals) to assess whether having children is associated with lower engagement in extramarital affairs. I then fit a logistic regression predicting whether the respondent had any affair from children status while adjusting for available covariates (age, yearsmarried, religiousness, education, rating) to reduce confounding. The coefficient for having children (C(children)[T.yes]) on the log-odds scale was -0.019 with a 95% confidence interval [-0.433, 0.395], corresponding to an odds ratio of approximately 0.98. This negative coefficient and odds ratio below 1 indicate that, in this sample, having children is associated with a lower likelihood of engaging in extramarital affairs, even after accounting for the included covariates.

Using the 601 observations in the dataset, I compared extramarital affairs between marriages with and without children. First, simple group summaries show that people without children report slightly more affairs on average: the mean affairs score is about 1.69 for couples without children versus about 1.36 for couples with children, and the share having any affair is about 25.7% without children and 24.7% with children. The difference in the probability of having any affair is therefore very small (roughly a 1 percentage‑point drop when children are present), but the average number of affairs among all respondents is notably lower when children are present. To adjust for other factors that might be related to affairs, I fit a Poisson regression of the affair count on an indicator for having children plus controls for age, years married, religiousness, education, occupation, and self‑rated marriage quality. In this model, the coefficient on having children is negative (around -0.24) and statistically significant (p≈0.001), implying that, holding these other variables fixed, marriages with children have roughly 20% fewer affairs on average (exp(-0.24) ≈ 0.79). A logistic regression for whether someone has any affair (yes/no) shows an effect of children that is very close to zero and not statistically significant, which confirms that children do not meaningfully change the chance of having at least one affair but are associated with somewhat fewer affair incidents overall. Taken together, these results provide moderate evidence that, in this sample, having children is associated with a modest decrease in overall engagement in extramarital affairs, though the effect is not dramatic and the data are limited to this specific survey population.

Among those with children (n = 430), the mean affairs score was about 1.36 and about 24.7% reported at least one affair. To formally test the relationship between children and the likelihood of any affair, I fit a logistic regression model with any-affair (yes/no) as the outcome and children (yes/no) as the predictor. The coefficient for having children was slightly negative (log-odds coefficient ≈ -0.057), indicating a tiny tendency toward fewer affairs among people with children, but this effect was far from statistically significant (p ≈ 0.783). Given the small effect sizes and the very high p-value, the data do not provide convincing evidence that having children meaningfully decreases engagement in extramarital affairs. At best, the data are consistent with no real effect or only a very small decrease that is not distinguishable from random variation in this sample. Therefore, I answer "No" to the research question, with moderate strength and confidence: the observed differences are minor and statistically indistinguishable from zero, so the dataset does not support a clear claim that having children decreases extramarital affairs.

The raw affair rate was 25.7% for people without children (44/171) and 24.7% for people with children (106/430), a difference of only about 1 percentage point. A logistic regression of any_affair on children alone gave an odds ratio of 0.94 for having children versus not (95% CI 0.63–1.42, p = 0.78), and an adjusted model controlling for gender, age, years married, religiousness, education, occupation, and marital rating gave an odds ratio of 0.97 (95% CI 0.64–1.46, p = 0.87). Both models show a very small, statistically non-significant association with wide confidence intervals that include both modest decreases and increases. Therefore, this dataset does not provide reliable evidence that having children decreases engagement in extramarital affairs; if an effect exists, it is likely small and uncertain.

Using data from 601 married individuals, I compared extramarital affair engagement between those with and without children. The mean affairs score was about 1.36 for respondents with children versus 1.69 for those without, and the proportion reporting any affair was about 24.7% with children versus 25.7% without—a difference of only around one percentage point. Overall, the data do not support the claim that having children meaningfully decreases engagement in extramarital affairs; if an effect exists, it appears extremely small and indistinguishable from random variation in this sample.

Using 601 married respondents, those with children had slightly lower mean affair counts (1.36 vs 1.69) and a very similar proportion reporting any affair (24.7% vs 25.7%). Chi-square and Mann-Whitney tests found no statistically significant association between having children and either the presence or frequency of affairs (p-values around 0.86 and 0.62). A logistic regression of having any affair on children status plus age, years married, religiousness, education, occupation, marital rating and gender estimated an odds ratio of about 0.97 for parents versus non-parents (95% confidence interval roughly 0.64 to 1.46, p about 0.87), indicating an effect close to zero and highly uncertain. Using the 601 observations in the affairs dataset, I compared extramarital-affair engagement between people with and without children. First, simple group means show that individuals without children report an average affairs score of about 1.69, whereas those with children report about 1.36, implying roughly a 20% lower level of affairs among parents. The proportion of respondents having any extramarital affair at all is very similar (about 25.7% with no children vs. 24.7% with children), so having children does not materially change whether someone has at least one affair. To account for other factors, I ran a logistic regression for the probability of any affair (dependent variable: indicator of any affairs; predictors: children plus gender, age, years married, religiousness, education, occupation, and marital-rating). In that model, the coefficient on having children is essentially zero and clearly not statistically significant (p ≈ 0.87), reinforcing that children do not meaningfully change the chance of having at least one affair. I then modeled the count/intensity of affairs using a Poisson regression with the same controls. In this model, the coefficient on having children is negative and statistically significant (≈ -0.24 with p ≈ 0.001), which corresponds to parents having about 20–25% fewer expected affairs (exp(-0.24) ≈ 0.79) than comparable non-parents, conditional on the same demographic and relationship characteristics. Taken together, the evidence indicates that having children does not strongly affect whether someone has any extramarital relationship, but it is associated with a modest, statistically significant reduction in the overall intensity (number/frequency) of extramarital affairs. Therefore, I conclude that having children does decrease engagement in extramarital affairs, but the effect is modest rather than large, which is reflected in the moderate strength and confidence scores reported here.

Using the 601 married respondents in this dataset, I first defined a binary outcome indicating whether each person reported any extramarital affair in the past year. Descriptively, people without children had a mean affair score of about 1.69 and 25.7% reported at least one affair, whereas people with children had a mean affair score of about 1.36 and 24.7% reported any affair. I then fit a logistic regression model with any-affair status as the outcome and children status, gender, age, years married, religiousness, education, occupation, and self-rated marital happiness as predictors. The coefficient for having children (yes versus no) was approximately -0.03 on the log-odds scale, corresponding to an odds ratio of about 0.97 with a p-value around 0.87 and a wide confidence interval that comfortably includes both modest decreases and modest increases in odds. This indicates no statistically or practically meaningful association between having children and the likelihood of engaging in an extramarital affair in this sample, even after adjusting for key covariates. Taken together, both the descriptive comparisons and the regression analysis fail to provide evidence that having children decreases engagement in extramarital affairs; the data are most consistent with little to no effect of children on affair involvement.

Using the provided dataset (601 currently married individuals), I treated the `age` column as the coded frequency of extramarital intercourse during the past year (0 = none, 1 = once, 2 = twice, 3 = three times, 7 = 4–10 times, 12 = monthly/weekly/daily) as indicated in the metadata, and constructed a binary indicator `has_affair` for any extramarital intercourse (age > 0). Therefore, I conclude that the data do not provide strong evidence that having children decreases engagement in extramarital affairs, leading to a “No” answer with moderately strong backing but high confidence in the lack of a meaningful effect.

The dataset contains 601 married individuals with a variable encoding how often they engaged in extramarital sexual intercourse in the past year and a yes/no indicator for whether there are children in the marriage. Using the 601-person dataset, I compared affair frequency (coded in the 'age' column) between people with and without children (from the 'religiousness' yes/no indicator) and found only very small, non-significant differences: mean affair frequency was about 1.36 with children vs 1.69 without, and the proportion with any affair was about 24.7% with children vs 25.7% without (Welch t-test p ≈ 0.30, chi-squared test p ≈ 0.86). Using 1450 tooth class observations from humans and three non human primate genera, I modeled the probability that a socket shows antemortem tooth loss with binomial regression at the tooth level, including genus, age, sex (probability male), and tooth class as predictors. Descriptively, overall AMTL rates were about 6.5% in Homo sapiens, 6.9% in Pan, 7.6% in Papio, and 4.4% in Pongo (total missing teeth divided by total sockets). In the regression with Homo sapiens as the reference genus, Pan and Papio had slightly positive but non significant genus coefficients, while Pongo had a significantly negative coefficient (log odds around -0.37, p about 0.02), indicating substantially lower AMTL odds than humans after adjusting for age, sex, and tooth class. Age, sex, and tooth class effects were small and not statistically significant. Because at least one non human genus (Pongo) clearly has lower AMTL than humans and the others are statistically indistinguishable from humans rather than consistently lower, the data do not support the claim that modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than non human primate genera after accounting for these covariates.

Using the AMTL dataset of 1,450 specimen-tooth-class observations, I compared the number of missing teeth to the number of observable sockets for modern humans and three non-human primate genera. Tooth-weighted AMTL rates were 6.5% for Homo sapiens (565/8673 sockets) versus 6.7% for the pooled non-human primates (324/4857 sockets), indicating similar or slightly lower AMTL in humans. A binomial logistic regression of AMTL counts on an indicator for Homo sapiens, adjusting for age, sex (probability of being male), and tooth class, yielded an odds ratio of 0.98 for humans versus non-humans (log-odds -0.023, SE 0.072, p = 0.75), and adjusted predicted AMTL probabilities differed by less than 0.2 percentage points across tooth classes. Together, these results provide no evidence that modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than non-human primates; if anything, humans show marginally lower rates, but the difference is not statistically significant.

Using a binomial regression model for AMTL proportion (missing teeth over observable sockets) with a logit link and sockets as trial weights, and adjusting for age, probability of being male, and tooth class, modern humans do not show consistently higher AMTL frequencies than the non-human primate genera. Standardized predicted AMTL proportions are about 0.065 for Homo sapiens, 0.069 for Pan, 0.077 for Papio, and 0.043 for Pongo, so humans are slightly lower than Pan and Papio but higher than Pongo. Genus coefficients relative to humans indicate no significant difference for Pan, a marginally higher rate for Papio, and a significantly lower rate for Pongo, leading to an overall pattern that contradicts the claim that humans broadly have higher AMTL than these non-human primates.

Using the AMTL dataset of 1,450 tooth-class observations (928 human and 522 non-human), I modeled the probability of antemortem tooth loss as a binomial outcome (number of missing teeth out of observable sockets) using a logistic regression with a logit link. The model included an indicator for modern humans (Homo sapiens vs. Pan/Pongo/Papio), age at death, sex (probability of male), and tooth class (anterior, posterior, premolar) as predictors, with sockets used as binomial weights. The fitted human indicator coefficient was very close to zero and slightly negative (log-odds coefficient around -0.02, odds ratio about 0.98) with a very large p-value (~0.75), indicating no statistically reliable increase in AMTL for humans once age, sex, and tooth class are accounted for. Counterfactual predictions from the model showed nearly identical mean predicted AMTL probabilities for humans (about 6.5%) and non-human primates (about 6.7%), and the raw observed proportions of missing teeth per socket were also almost the same for humans and non-humans. Taken together, these results imply that modern humans do not exhibit higher frequencies of antemortem tooth loss than the non-human primate genera in this sample after controlling for age, sex, and tooth class.

I modeled the proportion of antemortem tooth loss (AMTL) per specimen and tooth-class using a binomial regression with a logit link. Each row was weighted by the number of observable sockets, and I used cluster-robust standard errors grouped by specimen ID (feature2) to partly account for repeated observations per individual.

The fitted model coefficient for the human indicator (Homo sapiens vs. non-human primates) was -0.008 on the log-odds scale, corresponding to an odds ratio of 0.99 with a 95% confidence interval from 0.74 to 1.33 and a p-value of 0.956. Positive values indicate higher odds of AMTL for modern humans after adjusting for age, sex, and tooth class, while negative values indicate lower odds.

I first fit a binomial generalized linear model (logit link) to specimen-level proportions of missing teeth (missing teeth / observable sockets) with the number of observable sockets as frequency weights. In this model, the coefficient for the human indicator (is_human) was approximately -0.019 on the log-odds scale, corresponding to an odds ratio of about 0.98, with a 95% confidence interval that spanned from roughly 0.85 to 1.13 and a large p-value (~0.79). I fit a binomial logistic regression for the proportion of antemortem tooth loss (num_amtl / sockets) with genus, age at death, sex (prob_male), and tooth class as predictors, weighting each observation by the number of observable sockets. In this dataset of 1450 tooth-class observations, humans have an overall AMTL rate of about 0.065 missing teeth per socket compared with higher rates in Pan (0.069) and Papio (0.076) and a lower rate in Pongo (0.044). A binomial logistic regression modeling the proportion of missing teeth (num_amtl / sockets) with a logit link and predictors for genus, age, sex (prob_male), and tooth class, using cluster-robust standard errors by specimen, shows no significant positive effect for humans: the human indicator coefficient is approximately -0.02 with a p-value around 0.90, and genus contrasts relative to humans are also non-significant. Predicted AMTL probabilities at median age, mean sex probability, and the modal tooth class are about 0.067 for humans versus roughly 0.071 for Pan and 0.077 for Papio. I analyzed antemortem tooth loss (AMTL) using binomial regression on the counts of missing teeth and observable sockets for modern humans (Homo sapiens) and three non-human primate genera (Pan, Pongo, Papio). I then fit a generalized linear model with a binomial family where the response was the proportion of missing teeth, the trial count was the number of sockets, and predictors included a binary indicator for humans versus non-humans, estimated age at death, sex estimate, and tooth class (anterior, posterior, premolar). The coefficient for the human indicator corresponded to an odds ratio of 0.98, with a p-value of 0.793, and the average marginal effect of being human on the probability of AMTL across the observed covariate distribution was -0.001. Based on the direction and magnitude of this effect, along with its statistical significance and the descriptive differences in AMTL frequencies, I concluded a 'No' answer to the research question, with a strength of 0 out of 100 and a confidence of 45 out of 100.

Research question: "Do modern humans (Homo sapiens) have higher frequencies of antemortem tooth loss (AMTL) compared to non-human primate genera (Pan, Pongo, Papio), after accounting for the effects of age, sex, and tooth class?" I used the provided AMTL dataset of 1450 specimen–tooth-class records to address this. Because the column names were shuffled, I first remapped them so that tooth class (anterior/posterior/premolar), genus (Homo sapiens, Pan, Papio, Pongo), the count of missing teeth, the number of observable sockets, estimated age at death, and an ordinal sex-code variable were correctly interpreted. I then modeled the proportion of teeth lost antemortem (number of missing teeth divided by the number of observable sockets for each specimen and tooth class) using a binomial regression with a logit link. The model included genus, age at death, sex code, and tooth class as predictors and used the number of observable sockets as binomial frequency weights so that each tooth contributed equally. After removing a small number of impossible records where the number of missing teeth exceeded the number of observable sockets, the cleaned dataset contained 1430 rows, representing roughly 13422 individual teeth. Descriptively, genus-level AMTL frequencies (missing teeth divided by observable sockets) were very similar across groups: Homo sapiens ≈ 0.054, Pan ≈ 0.065, Papio ≈ 0.052, and Pongo ≈ 0.044. In the regression that contrasted humans against all non-human primates while adjusting for age, sex, and tooth class, the coefficient for the human indicator was -0.008 on the log-odds scale with a p-value of 0.918 and a 95% confidence interval from -0.164 to 0.148, indicating an effect indistinguishable from zero. At typical covariate values (mean age, mean sex-code, and a representative tooth class), the adjusted predicted AMTL probability was about 0.052 for Homo sapiens and 0.053 for non-human primates, a difference of -0.000 in absolute probability. Because humans did not have the highest AMTL frequencies in the descriptive summaries and the adjusted human effect in the regression was essentially zero and not statistically significant, the data do not support the claim that modern humans have higher frequencies of antemortem tooth loss than the non-human primate genera once age, sex, and tooth class are taken into account.

Using 420 California school districts, I constructed a student teacher ratio as students divided by teachers and an average test score as the mean of reading and math scores. The simple correlation between the ratio and test scores was essentially zero (r ≈ 0.02), and a linear regression of test scores on the ratio yielded an almost zero slope (about 0.001 points per one unit change in the ratio) with a very large p-value (around 0.67) and R-squared below 0.001. Adding key demographic controls (income, percent English learners, and percent on subsidized lunch) did not materially change the estimate or its non-significance. Together, these results indicate that, in this dataset, there is no meaningful evidence that lower student teacher ratios are associated with higher academic performance.

A simple OLS regression of performance on the ratio yielded a coefficient of roughly 0.001 score points per additional student per teacher (95% confidence interval approximately −0.004 to 0.006, p ≈ 0.67, R² ≈ 0.000), so lower ratios are not associated with higher scores and any effect, if present, is extremely small. Adding controls for income, English-learner share, poverty measures, computers, and per-pupil expenditures barely changed the coefficient (still about 0.001 with p ≈ 0.68 and R² ≈ 0.006), indicating that adjusting for these covariates does not reveal a hidden association. Restricting the analysis to observations with more typical student–teacher ratios (≤ 30 or ≤ 50 students per teacher) also produced very small positive correlations (around 0.06), reinforcing the conclusion that within this dataset lower student–teacher ratios are not meaningfully associated with higher academic performance.

The strength score of 2 reflects the magnitude of the correlation between the ratio and test scores, and the confidence score of 33 reflects the limited statistical evidence (relatively large p-value) for an association in this sample.

Research question: Is a lower student–teacher ratio associated with higher academic performance (measured by the average of reading and math scores) across California K–6/K–8 school districts.

The analysis uses 420 districts with complete data. I constructed the student–teacher ratio as 'students / teachers' and the academic performance measure as the average of reading and math test scores.

First, I examined the simple Pearson correlation between the student–teacher ratio and average test score. The correlation is 0.021, indicating that districts with more students per teacher (larger ratios) tend to have slightly higher test scores (a positive association), although the magnitude is very small.

Second, I estimated a simple linear regression of average test score on the student–teacher ratio. The estimated coefficient on the ratio is 0.001, with a p-value of 0.6728 and an R-squared of 0.000. This slope is not statistically different from zero at conventional significance levels, so the data do not show a clear linear relationship.

Third, I estimated a multiple regression that adds key demographic and socioeconomic controls (family income, percentage of English learners, percentage on reduced-price lunch, and percentage on public assistance). In this model, the coefficient on the student–teacher ratio is 0.001 with a p-value of 0.6575 and an R-squared of 0.003. The coefficient is not statistically significant after adding these controls, indicating that once we adjust for demographics and income, there is still no clear linear relationship.

Taken together, the near-zero correlation and regression coefficients that are small in magnitude and not statistically significant suggest that, in this dataset, there is not strong evidence that lower student–teacher ratios are associated with higher academic performance. Any true effect, if it exists, is likely modest relative to other district-level factors such as demographics and income, and cannot be distinguished clearly from noise with these data.
